facts.statement: The name Styracosaurus means "spiked lizard" derived from Ancient Greek words for a spike and a lizard.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus ( ; meaning "spiked lizard" from the Ancient Greek styrax/στύραξ "spike at the butt-end of a spear-shaft" and sauros/σαῦρος "lizard")

facts.statement: Styracosaurus possessed four to six long spikes on its neck frill, cheek horns, and a single nose horn that could reach 60 cm in length and 15 cm in width.
facts.quote: It had four to six long parietal spikes extending from its neck frill, a smaller jugal horn on each of its cheeks, and a single horn protruding from its nose, which may have been up to 60 cm long and 15 cm wide.

facts.statement: This dinosaur grew to lengths between 5 and 5.5 meters and weighed approximately 1.8 to 2.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus was a relatively large dinosaur, reaching lengths of 5 - 5.5 m and weighing about 1.8 - 2.7 MT.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus stood about 1.8 meters tall at the shoulder.
facts.quote: It stood about 1.8 m tall.

facts.statement: The dinosaur had a relatively short tail.
facts.quote: Its tail was rather short.

facts.statement: Its skull featured a beak and shearing cheek teeth in continuous dental batteries, indicating a diet of sliced plants.
facts.quote: The skull had a beak and shearing cheek teeth arranged in continuous dental batteries, suggesting that the animal sliced up plants.

facts.statement: Evidence from bone beds suggests Styracosaurus may have lived in large herds like other ceratopsians.
facts.quote: Like other ceratopsians, this dinosaur may have been a herd animal, travelling in large groups, as suggested by bone beds.

facts.statement: The genus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is classified as a member of the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus is a member of the Centrosaurinae.

facts.statement: This extinct herbivorous dinosaur lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus ( ; meaning "spiked lizard" from the Ancient Greek styrax/στύραξ "spike at the butt-end of a spear-shaft" and sauros/σαῦρος "lizard") is an extinct genus of herbivorous dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian stage) of North America.

facts.statement: The first fossil was discovered in the summer of 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg during a Geological Survey of Canada expedition along the Red Deer River.
facts.quote: The first fossil of Styracosaurus was discovered in the summer of 1913 by American palaeontologist Charles H. Sternberg as part of an expedition of the Geological Survey of Canada along the Red Deer River.

facts.statement: The initial skull discovery occurred on the southwest bank of the Red Deer River, approximately 12 miles below the mouth of Berry Creek in the Belly River Formation.
facts.quote: Sternberg discovered the skull on the southwest bank of the Red Deer River about 12 mi below the mouth of Berry Creek in what was then called the Belly River Formation.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe described the mostly complete skull found by Sternberg in 1913 as the holotype of Styracosaurus albertensis.
facts.quote: This mostly complete skull was described in 1913 by Canadian palaeontologist Lawrence Lambe as the holotype of the new ceratopsian Styracosaurus albertensis.

facts.statement: The site where the original fossils were found is now located within Dinosaur Provincial Park in the Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: The quarry and sediments are now within the boundaries of Dinosaur Provincial Park and the Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: In 1955, the Canadian Museum of Nature acquired the mandible and skeleton, reuniting the full type specimen which is now cataloged as CMN 344.
facts.quote: Negotiations concluded in 1955 allowing the Canadian Museum of Nature to acquire this mandible and skeleton, reuniting the full type individual of Styracosaurus, now under the accession number CMN 344.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown collected another specimen in 1915 from the middle fork of Sand Creek, 12 miles downstream of Steveville.
facts.quote: American palaeontologist Barnum Brown collected another specimen of Styracosaurus in 1915 from the same horizon as the type, but from the middle fork of Sand Creek 12 mi downstream of Steveville.

facts.statement: The species name S. parksi honors the Canadian palaeontologist William Parks, who assisted in comparing the new specimen with S. albertensis.
facts.quote: The species name was in honour of the late Canadian palaeontologist William Parks, who helped Brown and Schlaijker compare their specimen with the skeleton of S. albertensis that was at the time at the University of Toronto.

facts.statement: The specific locality where S. parksi was found was relocated in 2006 by Darren Tanke in the upper Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: in 2006 it was relocated by Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology in the upper portion of the Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: A nearly complete skull and skeleton of S. albertensis was found in 1989 at Sage Creek, about 130 km southeast of the holotype, making it the only definitive specimen of that species outside Dinosaur Provincial Park.
facts.quote: A nearly complete skull and skeleton (TMP 1989.97.1) was found in 1989 at Sage Creek only 10 m below the prairie level in the coulee, but approximately 130 km southeast of the holotype and the only definitive specimen of Styracosaurus albertensis from outside Dinosaur Provincial Park.

facts.statement: A large Styracosaurus skeleton was found in May 2015 near Duchess, Alberta, and excavated over three years by the University of Alberta.
facts.quote: In May 2015 a skeleton of a large Styracosaurus was found along Matzhiwin Creek near the town of Duchess, Alberta around 18 km west of Dinosaur Provincial Park by the University of Alberta and excavated over three years.

facts.statement: The classification of S. ovatus is debated, having been moved to Rubeosaurus in 2010 but considered again as a species of Styracosaurus or even S. albertensis since 2020.
facts.quote: Another species, S. ovatus, named in 1930 by Charles Gilmore was reassigned to a new genus, Rubeosaurus, by Andrew McDonald and Jack Horner in 2010, but it has been considered either its own genus or a species of Styracosaurus (or even a specimen of S. albertensis) again, since 2020.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus albertensis measured approximately 5.5 to 5.8 meters in length and stood about 1.65 meters high at the hips.
facts.quote: These fossils indicate that S. albertensis was around 5.5-5.8 m in length and stood about 1.65 m high at the hips.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests the frill of the holotype specimen broke during the animal's life and was shortened by approximately 6 centimeters.
facts.quote: It appears that the frill suffered a break at this point in life and was shortened by about 6 cm.

facts.statement: Fossils of Styracosaurus have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation near Steveville, Alberta.
facts.quote: These fossils were also found in the Dinosaur Park Formation, near Steveville, Alberta.

facts.statement: Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum relocated the lost site of S. parksi in the summer of 2006.
facts.quote: In the summer of 2006, Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology in Drumheller, Alberta relocated the long lost S. parksi site.

facts.statement: Specimens initially described as S. parksi were distinguished from S. albertensis by having a different cheekbone shape and smaller tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: Among the differences between the specimens cited by Brown and Schlaikjer were a cheekbone quite different from that of S. albertensis, and smaller tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: The species S. parksi is now generally accepted as a specimen of S. albertensis.
facts.quote: It is now accepted as a specimen of S. albertensis.

facts.statement: Pieces of the skull originally found in 1915 were later discovered in the quarry, evidently abandoned by the initial collecting crew.
facts.quote: Pieces of the skull, evidently abandoned by the 1915 crew, were found in the quarry.

facts.statement: Bonebed 42 contains numerous skull fragments, including horncores, jaws, and frill pieces.
facts.quote: Bonebed 42 is known to contain numerous pieces of skulls such as horncores, jaws and frill pieces.

facts.statement: S. sphenocerus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius and later attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.
facts.quote: S. sphenocerus, described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius and based on a nasal bone with a broken Styracosaurus-like straight nose horn, was attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.

facts.statement: The informal name S. makeli, mentioned by Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas in 1990, is an early name for the genus Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: "S. makeli", mentioned informally by amateur paleontologists Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas in 1990 in a caption to an illustration, is an early name for Einiosaurus.

facts.statement: S. borealis was an early informal name for S. parksi.
facts.quote: "S. borealis" is an early informal name for S. parksi.

facts.statement: Unlike S. albertensis, the longest parietal spikes of S. ovatus converge towards their tips rather than projecting parallel behind the frill.
facts.quote: Unlike S. albertensis, the longest parietal spikes converge towards their tips, instead of projecting parallel behind the frill.

facts.statement: The spikes of S. ovatus were much shorter than those of S. albertensis, with the longest measuring only 295 millimeters.
facts.quote: As estimated from the preserved material, the spikes are much shorter than in S. albertensis, with the longest only 295 mm long.

facts.statement: McDonald and Horner reclassified S. ovatus into the new genus Rubeosaurus based on phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: McDonald and Horner gave the species the new genus name Rubeosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Robert Holmes and colleagues found that the type specimen of Rubeosaurus ovatus falls within the morphological variation of S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Robert Holmes and colleagues in 2020 found that USNM 11869, the type specimen of Rubeosaurus ovatus, fell within the variation seen in other specimens from the older deposits of the Dinosaur Park Formation S. albertensis is known from.

facts.statement: Holmes and colleagues considered S. ovatus to be a junior synonym of S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Holmes et al. considering the latter a junior synonym of the former.

facts.statement: Wilson and colleagues advised retaining S. ovatus as a separate species of Styracosaurus, likely directly descended from S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Wilson and colleagues advised that S. ovatus was retained as a separate, probably directly descended from S. albertensis, species of Styracosaurus.

facts.statement: The specimen USNM 14768 was considered too immature to be diagnostic, limiting the species S. ovatus to its holotype USNM 11869.
facts.quote: The immature specimen USNM 14768, referred to S. ovatus by McDonald et al. in 2011, was considered too immature to be diagnostic, and thus S. ovatus was limited to its holotype USNM 11869.

facts.statement: Adult Styracosaurus measured between 5 and 5.5 meters in length and weighed between 1.8 and 2.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Individuals of the genus Styracosaurus were approximately 5 - 5.5 m long as adults and weighed about 1.8 - 2.7 MT.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus possessed a massive skull featuring a tall straight nasal horn and a neck frill adorned with at least four large spikes.
facts.quote: The skull was massive, with a large nostril, a tall straight nose horn, and a parietal squamosal frill (a neck frill) crowned with at least four large spikes.

facts.statement: The four longest spikes on the neck frill of Styracosaurus were 50 to 55 centimeters long, similar in size to its nasal horn.
facts.quote: Each of the four longest frill spines was comparable in length to the nose horn, at 50 to 55 cm long.

facts.statement: Lambe estimated the nasal horn of the type specimen to be 57 centimeters long, though the actual tip was missing from the fossil.
facts.quote: The nasal horn was estimated by Lambe at 57 cm long in the type specimen, but the tip had not been preserved.

facts.statement: Subadult Styracosaurus had modest pyramid-shaped brow horns that were replaced by pits in adults.
facts.quote: Modest pyramid-shaped brow horns were present in subadults, but were replaced by pits in adults.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a toothless beak at the front of its mouth.
facts.quote: The front of the mouth had a toothless beak.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had powerful shoulders that may have been used in combat with other individuals of its species.
facts.quote: It had powerful shoulders which may have been useful in intraspecies combat.

facts.statement: Each toe of Styracosaurus ended in a hoof-like claw sheathed in horn.
facts.quote: Each toe bore a hooflike ungual which was sheathed in horn.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests that Styracosaurus likely held its legs in an intermediate crouched position rather than sprawling or standing straight.
facts.quote: The most recent work has put forward an intermediate crouched position as most likely.

facts.statement: There is significant debate regarding the validity of certain centrosaurine genera, including whether Centrosaurus and Monoclonius are distinct genera, undiagnosable, or represent sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: Because of the variation between species and even individual specimens of centrosaurines, there has been much debate over which genera and species are valid, particularly whether Centrosaurus and/or Monoclonius are valid genera, undiagnosable, or possibly members of the opposite sex.

facts.statement: Most researchers do not accept Monoclonius nasicornis as a female Styracosaurus, considering it instead a synonym of Centrosaurus apertus.
facts.quote: However, most other researchers have not accepted Monoclonius nasicornis as a female Styracosaurus, instead regarding it as a synonym of Centrosaurus apertus.

facts.statement: A bone bed containing Styracosaurus remains has been discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
facts.quote: A bone bed composed of Styracosaurus remains is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, about halfway up the formation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the mass death of Styracosaurus at the Dinosaur Park Formation site may have occurred when non-herding animals gathered around a waterhole during a drought in a seasonal, semi-arid environment.
facts.quote: The mass deaths at this site may have been a result of otherwise non-herding animals congregating around a waterhole in a period of drought, with evidence suggesting the environment may have been seasonal and semi-arid.

facts.statement: Paleontologists Gregory Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that Styracosaurus could run faster than an elephant based on trackway evidence lacking sprawling forelimb signs.
facts.quote: Paleontologists Gregory Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that large ceratopsians such as Styracosaurus were able to run faster than an elephant, based on possible ceratopsian trackways which did not exhibit signs of sprawling forelimbs.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus were herbivores that likely fed mostly on low-growing vegetation due to the position of their heads.
facts.quote: Styracosaurs were herbivorous dinosaurs; they probably fed mostly on low growth because of the position of the head.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus may have been capable of knocking down taller plants using their horns, beak, and large body size.
facts.quote: They may, however, have been able to knock down taller plants with their horns, beak, and bulk.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had teeth arranged in batteries where older upper teeth were continually replaced by newer ones underneath.
facts.quote: Ceratopsid teeth, including those of Styracosaurus, were arranged in groups called batteries. Older teeth on top were continually replaced by the teeth underneath them.

facts.statement: Unlike hadrosaurids, the dental batteries of Styracosaurus were adapted for slicing rather than grinding food.
facts.quote: Unlike hadrosaurids, which also had dental batteries, ceratopsid teeth sliced but did not grind.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the specific diet of Styracosaurus, with some scientists suggesting they ate palms and cycads while others propose ferns.
facts.quote: Some scientists have suggested that ceratopsids like Styracosaurus ate palms and cycads, while others have suggested ferns.

facts.statement: Peter Dodson proposed that Late Cretaceous ceratopsians like Styracosaurus may have knocked down angiosperm trees to shear off leaves and twigs.
facts.quote: Dodson has proposed that Late Cretaceous ceratopsians may have knocked down angiosperm trees and then sheared off leaves and twigs.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that the lineage leading to Styracosaurus originated in Asia during the Jurassic, with true horned ceratopsians appearing in North America by the early Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: These new discoveries have been important in illuminating the origins of horned dinosaurs in general, and suggest that the group originated during the Jurassic in Asia, with the appearance of true horned ceratopsians occurring by the beginning of the late Cretaceous in North America.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Styracosaurus displaced its relative Centrosaurus as environmental conditions changed over time.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus is known from a higher position in the formation (relating specifically to its own genus) than the closely related Centrosaurus, suggesting that Styracosaurus displaced Centrosaurus as the environment changed over time and/or dimension.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus possessed large nasal horns and frills that were among the most distinctive facial features of all dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The large nasal horns and frills of Styracosaurus are among the most distinctive facial adornments of all dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The function of Styracosaurus horns and frills has been debated since the discovery of the first horned dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Their function has been the subject of debate since the first horned dinosaurs were discovered.

facts.statement: Researchers long believed Styracosaurus used its frills and horns for defense against large predatory dinosaurs.
facts.quote: It was long believed that ceratopsians like Styracosaurus used their frills and horns in defence against the large predatory dinosaurs of the time.

facts.statement: A 2006 study found no evidence that skull damage in ceratopsians was caused by horn thrust injuries during combat.
facts.quote: a 2006 study found no evidence for horn thrust injuries causing these forms of damage

facts.statement: The large frill of Styracosaurus may have helped regulate body temperature by increasing surface area, similar to elephant ears.
facts.quote: The large frill on Styracosaurus and related genera also may have helped to increase body area to regulate body temperature, like the ears of the modern elephant.

facts.statement: The extravagant variation in ceratopsid frills suggests that visual display is the primary function of these structures.
facts.quote: This observation is highly suggestive of what is now believed to be the primary function, display.

facts.statement: Marked differences in horned dinosaur adornments suggest visual displays were important for courtship or social behavior.
facts.quote: Evidence that visual display was important, either in courtship or in other social behavior, can be seen in the fact that horned dinosaurs differ markedly in their adornments, making each species highly distinctive.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that exaggerated dinosaur structures were used for species identification is questioned because this function is rare in modern tetrapods.
facts.quote: The use of the exaggerated structures in dinosaurs as species identification has been questioned, as no such function exists in vast majority of modern species of tetrapods

facts.statement: A 2015 skull discovery suggests that individual variation in Styracosaurus horn asymmetry was likely commonplace.
facts.quote: A skull discovered in 2015 from a Styracosaurus indicates that individual variation was likely commonplace in the genus.

facts.statement: The genus Styracosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Lambe, 1913

facts.statement: The species Styracosaurus albertensis was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: species_authority: Lambe, 1913

facts.statement: Centrosaurus nasicornis is listed as a synonym for Styracosaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Centrosaurus nasicornis Brown, 1917

facts.statement: Styracosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: Vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus was relatively large, reaching 5.5 meters in length, 1.8 meters in height, and weighing 2.4 tons.
facts.quote: Eran relativamente grandes, tenían 5,5 metros de longitud, 1,8 de altura y pesaban 2,4 toneladas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus had a beak and cutting molars arranged in continuous dental batteries, suggesting it cut plants.
facts.quote: Tenía un pico y muelas cortantes dispuestas en baterías dentales continuas, lo que sugiere que el animal cortaba plantas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus featured a notable cranial shield with four to six long parietal spikes extending from the neck, two jugal horns under the eyes, and one horn on the snout.
facts.quote: Su característica más notable es un escudo cefálico provisto de cuatro a seis púas parietales largas que se extendían desde el cuello, dos cuernos yugales bajo sus ojos y otro sobre su hocico.

facts.statement: The nasal horn of Styracosaurus could reach 60 centimeters in length and 15 centimeters in width.
facts.quote: este llegaba alcanzar 60 centímetros de largo y 15 de ancho.

facts.statement: The discovery of 100 individuals at an Arizona site indicates that Styracosaurus lived in herds like other ceratopsians.
facts.quote: En el yacimiento de Arizona se descubrieron 100 individuos, lo que indica que, como otros ceratópsidos, vivían en manadas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus fossils are known from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation

facts.statement: The Dinosaur Park Formation was a low-relief environment of rivers and floodplains that became swampy and influenced by marine conditions as the Western Interior Seaway expanded.
facts.quote: The Dinosaur Park Formation is interpreted as a low-relief setting of rivers and floodplains that became more swampy and influenced by marine conditions over time as the Western Interior Seaway transgressed westward.

facts.statement: The climate in the Dinosaur Park Formation was warmer than modern Alberta, without frost, but featured wetter and drier seasons.
facts.quote: The climate was warmer than present-day Alberta, without frost, but with wetter and drier seasons.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus ovatus lived alongside diverse fauna including hadrosaurids, centrosaurines, ankylosaurs, and the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus, which appears to have specialized in preying on ceratopsians.
facts.quote: In the Two Medicine Formation, dinosaurs that lived alongside Styracosaurus ovatus included the basal ornithopod Orodromeus, hadrosaurids (such as Hypacrosaurus, Maiasaura, and Prosaurolophus), the centrosaurines Brachyceratops and Einiosaurus, the leptoceratopsid Cerasinops, the ankylosaurs Edmontonia and Euoplocephalus, the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus (which appears to have been a specialist of preying on ceratopsians), as well as the smaller theropods Bambiraptor, Chirostenotes, Troodon, and Avisaurus.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is a ceratopsian dinosaur belonging to the subfamily Centrosaurinae and the tribe Centrosaurini.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus es un dinosaurio ceratópsido, miembro de la subfamilia Centrosaurinae y es originalmente también de pertenecen del su propia verdadera tribu que es Centrosaurini.

facts.statement: The species S. ovatus, named in 1930 by Charles Gilmore, was reassigned to the genus Rubeosaurus in 2010 by Andrew McDonald and Jack Horner, though it is now reconsidered as potentially belonging to Styracosaurus or S. albertensis.
facts.quote: Una segunda especie, S. ovatus, nombrada en 1930 por Charles Gilmore, fue reasignada a un nuevo género, Rubeosaurus, por Andrew McDonald y Jack Horner en 2010, aunque recientemente se ha considerado nuevamente que puede ser una especie de Styracosaurus o incluso un espécimen de S. albertensis.

facts.statement: Adult Styracosaurus measured approximately 5.5 meters in length and weighed about 2.7 tons.
facts.quote: Los individuos adultos del género Styracosaurus midieron aproximadamente 5,5 metros de largo cuando y pesaban de las 2,7 toneladas.

facts.statement: The skull was large and massive, featuring a large snout, a high nasal horn, and a frill topped with at least four long spikes.
facts.quote: El cráneo era grande y masivo, con un gran morro, con un cuerno en el hocico grande y alto, y una excrecencia parietoescamosa, la gola nucal, coronada con al menos 4 largas espinas.

facts.statement: Each of the neck spikes was comparable in length to the nasal horn, measuring between 50 and 55 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Cada una de estas espinas del cuello es comparable con las del hocico, de entre 50 a 55 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: The nasal horn is estimated to be 57 centimeters long in the holotype specimen, though it is only partially complete.
facts.quote: El cuerno nasal se estima en 57 centímetros en el espécimen holotipico, pero este cuerno solo esta parcialmente completo.

facts.statement: Small pyramid-shaped brow horns were present in subadults but were replaced by pits in adults.
facts.quote: Modestos cuernos en las cejas en forma de pirámide estaban presentes en los subadultos, pero fueron reemplazados por fosas en los adultos.

facts.statement: The front of the mouth had a toothless beak.
facts.quote: El frente de la boca tenía un pico desdentado.

facts.statement: The robust body of Styracosaurus resembles that of rhinoceroses.
facts.quote: El robusto cuerpo de Styracosaurus recuerda a los de los rinocerontes.

facts.statement: Each toe had a shape and structure similar to the hooves of modern ungulates, covered in keratin.
facts.quote: Cada dedo del pie tenía una forma y estructura similar al de los cascos de los ungulados modernos, forrado en queratina.

facts.statement: Recent work proposes an intermediate crouched posture as the most likely stance for Styracosaurus.
facts.quote: El trabajo más reciente ha propuesto una posición agachada intermedia como muy probable.

facts.statement: The first fossil remains of Styracosaurus were collected in Alberta, Canada, by C.M. Sternberg from the Dinosaur Park Formation and named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos fósiles de Styracosaurus fueron recogidos de Alberta, Canadá por C.M. Sternberg, del área hoy conocida como Parque Provincial del Dinosaurio, en la formación geológica actualmente conocida como Formación Dinosaur Park y nombrado por Lawrence Lambe en 1913.

facts.statement: The generic name is formed from the Greek words styrax, meaning 'spike' or 'thorn', and sauros, meaning 'lizard'.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico está formado por las palabras griegas στύραξ, styrax, —espina, púa— y σαῦρος, sauros, —lagarto—.

facts.statement: The specific epithet refers to the Latinized toponym of the Canadian province where the fossils were found, Alberta.
facts.quote: El epíteto específico hace referencia al topónimo latinizado del estado canadiense donde se hallaron sus restos fósiles, Alberta.

facts.statement: In the summer of 2006, Darren Tanke of the Tyrrell Museum in Drumheller, Alberta, rediscovered the original lost site of S. parksi.
facts.quote: En el verano de 2006, Darren Tanke del Museo Tyrrell en Drumheller, Alberta reencontraron el sitio original perdido de S. parksi.

facts.statement: Pieces of the skull, evidently abandoned by the 1915 team, were found at the site.
facts.quote: Pedazos del cráneo, abandonados evidentemente por el equipo 1915, fueron encontrados en el yacimiento.

facts.statement: At least one confirmed site, site 42, exists in the Provincial Dinosaur Park.
facts.quote: Al menos existe un yacimiento confirmado, yacimiento 42, en el Parque Provincial de los Dinosaurios

facts.statement: S. sphenocerus, described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius based on a nasal bone, was attributed to the straight nasal horn of a Styracosaurus in 1915.
facts.quote: S. sphenocerus, descrita por Edward Drinker Cope en 1890 como una especie de Monoclonius y basada en un hueso nasal, fue atribuido al cuerno recto de la nariz de un Styracosaurus, en 1915.

facts.statement: "S. makeli", mentioned informally by amateur paleontologists Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas in 1990 via a photo and illustration, is an early name for Einiosaurus.
facts.quote: "S. makeli", mencionada informalmente por los paleontólogos amateurs Stephen y Sylvia Czerkas en 1990 por una foto e ilustración, es un nombre temprano para Einiosaurus.

facts.statement: "S. borealis" is the informal name for S. parksi.
facts.quote: "S. borealis" es el nombre informal para S. parksi.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is known from a higher position in the formation than the closely related Centrosaurus, suggesting it was displaced by Centrosaurus when the environment changed in time and/or dimension.
facts.quote: Styracosaurus se conoce de una posición más alta en la formación, que se relaciona específicamente con su propio género, que el estrechamente vinculado Centrosaurus, sugiriendo que Styracosaurus fue desplazado por el Centrosaurus cuando el ambiente cambió en un cierto tiempo y/o dimensión.

facts.statement: A bone bed composed of Styracosaurus remains is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, halfway up the formation.
facts.quote: Un lecho de huesos compuesto por restos de Styracosaurus es conocido de la Formación Dinosaur Park de Alberta, a medio camino de la parte superior de la formación.

facts.statement: These mass deaths may have resulted from gathering solitary animals around a water hole during a drought, with evidence suggesting the environment may have been seasonal and semi-arid.
facts.quote: Estas muertes en masa pudieron haber sido también un resultado de reunir a animales solitarios alrededor de un hoyo de agua en un período de sequía, con evidencia que sugiere el ambiente pudo haber sido estacional y semiárido.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus were herbivorous dinosaurs that likely fed on low vegetation due to the head position.
facts.quote: Los Styracosaurus fueron dinosaurios herbívoros, que se alimentaban probablemente de la vegetación baja debido a la posición de la cabeza.

facts.statement: However, they may have been able to knock down taller plants with their horns, beak, and robust body.
facts.quote: Pudieron, sin embargo, haber podido derribado plantas más altas con sus cuernos, pico, y cuerpo robusto.

facts.statement: The jaws ended with a deep, narrow beak, believed to be better for stripping and defoliating than for biting.
facts.quote: Las quijadas terminaban con un pico profundo, estrecho, que se cree que habría sido mejor para arrnacar y deshojar que para morder.

facts.statement: The teeth of ceratopsians, including styracosaurians, were arranged in what have been called dental batteries.
facts.quote: Los dientes de los ceratópsidos, incluidos los de los estiracosaurios, se disponían en lo que se han llamado baterías dentales.

facts.statement: Some researchers have suggested that styracosaurians ate palms and cycads, while others propose they fed on ferns.
facts.quote: Algunos investigadores han sugerido que los estiracosaurios comían palmas y cycas, mientras que otros proponen que se alimentaban de helechos.

facts.statement: Dodson has proposed that Late Cretaceous ceratopsians may have knocked down angiosperm trees and then eaten the leaves and branches.
facts.quote: Dodson ha propuesto que los ceratopsianos de finales del Cretácico pudieron haber derribado árboles de angiospermas y entonces comido de las hojas y de las ramas.

facts.statement: Paleontologists Gregory S. Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that large ceratopsians like Styracosaurus could walk faster than an elephant, based on possible tracks showing no signs of forelimb extension.
facts.quote: Los paleontólogos Gregory S. Paul y Per Christiansen del Museo Zoológico de la Universidad de Copenhague en Dinamarca propusieron que los ceratopsianos grandes tales como Styracosaurus podían caminar más rápidamente que un elefante, basado en las posibles huellas de un ceratopsianos, el cual no exhibe muestras signos de esxteción de los miembros delanteros.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is distinguished by a long nasal horn and a large nuchal frill, which are the most distinctive facial ornaments of all dinosaurs.
facts.quote: El largo cuerno nasal y la gola nucal de los estiracosaurios son el más distintivo adorno facial de todos los dinosaurios.

facts.statement: The function of the nuchal frill in Styracosaurus has been debated since the first horned dinosaur was discovered.
facts.quote: Su función ha sido objeto de debate desde que el primer dinosaurio con cuerno ha sido encontrado.

facts.statement: R.S. Lull originally proposed that the nuchal frills of ceratopsians served as anchor points for powerful jaw muscles.
facts.quote: A principios del R. S. Lull propuso que las golas nucales de los ceratópsidos servián de anclaje a los poderosos músculos de las mandíbulas.

facts.statement: C.A. Forster found no evidence of large muscle insertions on the nuchal frill bones, challenging the muscle anchor hypothesis.
facts.quote: C.A. Forster, sin embargo no encontró evidencia de grandes inserciones musculares en los huesos de la gola nucal.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that bone resorption or unknown bone diseases, rather than combat, caused the damage patterns seen on Styracosaurus skulls.
facts.quote: En lugar, la resorción del hueso no patológico o las enfermedades desconocidas del hueso, se sugiere como causas.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that the large nuchal frill of Styracosaurus may have helped with thermoregulation by increasing surface area, similar to elephant ears.
facts.quote: La gran gola nucal vista en los estiracosaurios y sus parientes tal vez haya ayudado a incrementar el área corporal ayudando a la termorregulación, lcomo las orejas de los modernos elefantes.

facts.statement: The diversity of frill shapes suggests that the primary function of the nuchal frill in Styracosaurus was species recognition and display.
facts.quote: Esta diversidad de formas y arreglos hace pensar que la principal función era la exhibición y reconocimiento entre especies.

facts.statement: In 1961, Davitashvili proposed that the nuchal frill was used in courtship displays.
facts.quote: La teoría de que la gola nucal sea usada en la exhibición durante el cortejo fue propuesta en 1961 por Davitashvili.

facts.statement: A skull discovered in 2015 indicates that individual variation, such as asymmetrical horns, was common in the Styracosaurus genus.
facts.quote: Un cráneo descubierto en 2015 de un Styracosaurus indica que la variación individual probablemente era un lugar común en el género.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Styracosaurus belongs to the subfamily Centrosaurini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Centrosaurini

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is classified within the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Family: Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Styracosaurus is a member of the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: The Dinosaur Park Formation represents a low-relief environment of rivers and floodplains that became increasingly swampy and influenced by marine conditions over time.
facts.quote: La Formación Dinosaur Park se interpreta como un entorno de bajo relieve de ríos y llanuras aluviales que se volvieron más pantanosos e influenciados por las condiciones marinas con el tiempo

facts.statement: The climate in the Dinosaur Park Formation was warmer than modern Alberta, without frosts, but with distinct wet and dry seasons.
facts.quote: El clima era más cálido que el actual Alberta, sin heladas, pero con estaciones más húmedas y secas.

facts.statement: The vegetation in the Styracosaurus habitat likely consisted of a coniferous canopy with an understory of ferns, tree ferns, and angiosperms.
facts.quote: Aparentemente, las coníferas eran las plantas dominantes del dosel, con un sotobosque de helechos, helechos arborescentes y angiospermas.

facts.statement: Styracosaurus lived alongside a diverse fauna including other ceratopsians like Centrosaurus and Chasmosaurus, duck-billed dinosaurs like Prosaurolophus and Parasaurolophus, tyrannosaurids like Gorgosaurus and Daspletosaurus, and armored dinosaurs like Edmontonia and Euoplocephalus.
facts.quote: era miembro de una fauna diversa y bien documentada de animales prehistóricos que incluía parientes con cuernos como Centrosaurus y Chasmosaurus , dinosaurio de picos de pato como Prosaurolophus, Lambeosaurus, Gryposaurus , Corythosaurus y Parasaurolophus, tiranosáuridos Gorgosaurus , Daspletosaurus y los dinosaurios acorazados Edmontonia y Euoplocephalus.
